name: Remote Services
overview: Adversaries use valid accounts to authenticate to services that support remote connections — RDP, SMB, SSH, VNC, WinRM, DCOM, and their cloud equivalents — and once inside, use the built-in legitimate remote-access functionality of the operating system or cloud platform itself to move from host to host. This is the direct payoff of T1078: valid accounts establish that a credential works, T1021 is what an attacker actually does with network reach and that credential in hand. The 8 sub-techniques below split by protocol, not by sophistication — which one gets used is almost always a question of what's already open on the target, not which is more advanced.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Protocol choice is availability, not skill level
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: RDP, SSH, SMB, WinRM, VNC, and DCOM are not a ladder of increasing attacker sophistication — they're six different doors, and an intruder picks whichever one is already unlocked on this specific target. A Windows shop with RDP wide open gets RDP; a Linux-heavy environment gets SSH; a host with no remote GUI service at all but an open admin share gets SMB. This mirrors the interpreter-interchangeability idea from T1059: defending against just one of these protocols leaves the other five completely untouched.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Interactive vs. non-interactive access — different capability, different telemetry
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: RDP and VNC hand an attacker a full graphical session — they see what a user would see and can use any GUI tool already installed. SMB, WinRM, DCOM, and SSH give command execution without ever rendering a desktop. That split matters twice: it shapes what an attacker can accomplish immediately (GUI tooling vs. command-line only), and it shapes what shows up in logs — a RemoteInteractive logon behaves very differently from a scripted remote command, which is exactly why each sub-technique below has its own distinct detection fingerprint rather than one generic "remote logon" signal covering all of them.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Authentication proves identity; it rarely scopes what that identity can then do
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: Every protocol in this pack authenticates a connection — checks that the credential is real — but does comparatively little to restrict what an authenticated session can subsequently touch beyond coarse group membership (local admin, Domain Admins). That gap is exactly why network segmentation, RDP gateways, WinRM TrustedHosts scoping, and SSH allow-lists carry so much of the actual access-control weight in the mitigations below — the protocols themselves were largely never designed to do that job.

prerequisite_concepts.term: Cloud remote services: lateral movement without network adjacency
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: T1021.007 and T1021.008 extend this exact same valid-account-plus-remote-access pattern into infrastructure that has no traditional network boundary at all. A federated cloud identity can reach a console or VM connect feature from anywhere on the internet — an attacker doesn't need to be on the same network segment, or any network segment the victim controls, to "move laterally" in the cloud sense. That's a meaningful shift from everything else in this pack, where physical or logical network reach was always a precondition.

subtechniques.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
subtechniques.overview: RDP (Microsoft's Remote Desktop Services) gives an authenticated user a full interactive graphical session on a remote Windows host, using whatever privileges that account holds. Because it hands over a complete desktop rather than just command execution, it's one of the highest-capability lateral movement paths in this pack — and one of the most dangerous to expose directly to the internet, which is exactly what a large share of real-world ransomware intrusions still find open.

concepts.term: LogonType 10 as a clean, specific fingerprint
concepts.explanation: Windows logs an RDP session as Logon Type 10 (RemoteInteractive) in Security 4624 — a value that, unlike Type 3 (Network) or Type 2 (Interactive), is used almost exclusively for RDP. That specificity makes it one of the more reliable baseline-able signals in this whole guide: a RemoteInteractive logon for an account or at a time inconsistent with that account's normal pattern is worth a look far more often than a generic network logon would be.

concepts.term: Why full GUI access changes the risk calculus
concepts.explanation: Once an attacker has an RDP session, they don't need any additional tooling to be immediately productive — file explorer, a browser, whatever admin tools happen to be installed are all right there, exactly as a legitimate user would use them. That's precisely why internet-exposed RDP is treated as close to a hard no rather than a risk to be merely monitored: the cost of a successful compromise is a complete, no-extra-effort-required interactive session, not just a foothold.

concepts.term: Restricted Admin Mode: a hardening feature that opened its own Pass-the-Hash path
concepts.explanation: Restricted Admin Mode was introduced specifically to stop RDP from leaving reusable plaintext-equivalent credentials on the target by converting the session to a network logon (Type 3) instead of the usual RemoteInteractive (Type 10) logon. The side effect: because the server no longer needs the actual password, only proof of knowing it, an attacker holding just an NTLM hash can use Mimikatz's `sekurlsa::pth` to launch `mstsc.exe /restrictedadmin` and RDP into the target directly with the hash alone, no cracking required — turning a credential-protection feature into a new Pass-the-Hash delivery path, provided the target host has Restricted Admin Mode enabled and the attacker already holds local admin rights somewhere to extract the hash from.

procedure_examples.activity: Leveraged RDP for lateral movement and ransomware deployment.
Accessed domain controllers via RDP using compromised administrative privileges.
Deployed RDP for lateral movement during the campaign.
Moved laterally via RDP and exposed RDP ports using the NATBypass tool.
Includes commands for adding RDP users and establishing reverse SSH tunneling.

data_sources.detail: RemoteInteractive logon — the core RDP session-establishment signal.
Session reconnected / disconnected events, useful for tracking a session's full lifetime including hijacked or resumed sessions.
Inbound TCP 3389 connections, especially from an external IP if RDP is (or shouldn't be) internet-facing.

detection_queries.title: RemoteInteractive Logon Outside Normal Pattern
detection_queries.description: Flags LogonType 10 (RDP) sessions for an account, filterable further against that account's normal source/host baseline.
detection_queries.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624
| where LogonType == 10
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, IpAddress, WorkstationName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

detection_queries.title: RDP Logon from External or Unexpected Source
detection_queries.description: Vendor-agnostic RemoteInteractive logon detection, intended to be scoped with an allowlist of expected jump-host/admin sources.

title: RDP RemoteInteractive Logon

related.name: VNC

hypothesis.statement: A LogonType 10 (RemoteInteractive) session appears for an account, or from a source, that falls outside its established 30-day baseline.
hypothesis.rationale: Scope this hunt with an explicit allowlist of jump hosts and bastion servers from the outset -- without it, legitimate admin RDP traffic will dominate the result set and bury the hits worth investigating.

subtechniques.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
subtechniques.overview: Every Windows host exposes hidden administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) by default, reachable over SMB by anyone in the local Administrators group. Adversaries authenticate to these shares with valid credentials to copy files, then pair that file transfer with a second mechanism — a Scheduled Task, a Service, or WMI — to actually trigger execution, which is exactly what tools like PsExec and Impacket's smbexec automate end to end.

concepts.term: Admin shares are a feature, not a misconfiguration
concepts.explanation: C$, ADMIN$, and IPC$ exist on every Windows install by default specifically so administrators can manage a machine remotely without needing separate file-sharing infrastructure. Nothing about their presence indicates anything has gone wrong — which is exactly why disabling them is listed as its own mitigation rather than something to "fix": the tradeoff is real administrative convenience versus attack surface, not a bug to patch.

concepts.term: Copying a file over SMB doesn't execute it — that's a second step
concepts.explanation: Placing a binary on ADMIN$ via SMB is just a file transfer; nothing runs until something else triggers it. That's why the actual technique is almost always "SMB copy + Scheduled Task/Service/WMI execution" as a pair, not SMB alone — and why PsExec and smbexec bundle both steps into one tool. Detection built only around SMB share access misses half the story; the execution trigger that follows is just as important a signal.

procedure_examples.activity: Copied files to ADMIN$ shares for lateral movement.
Dropped a Cobalt Strike Beacon on domain controllers via SMB.
Accessed the ADMIN$ share via SMB for lateral movement.
Utilized net use commands to connect to network shares.
Leverages Admin$, C$, and IPC$ shares for propagation.

data_sources.detail: Network share object access, specifically to ADMIN$, C$, or IPC$ from a source host that isn't a known management/deployment system.
File creation over the network onto ADMIN$/C$, especially of an executable, immediately followed by a service or scheduled task referencing that same file.
New service (7045) or scheduled task (4698) creation shortly after SMB file transfer — the execution-trigger half of this two-step pattern.

detection_queries.title: Executable Written to Admin Share Followed by Service Creation
detection_queries.description: Flags the classic PsExec-style pattern: a file dropped on ADMIN$/C$ followed shortly by a new service referencing it.
detection_queries.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FolderPath has_any ("ADMIN$", "C$")
| where FileName endswith ".exe"
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceEvents
    | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
) on DeviceId
| where (ServiceInstalled_Timestamp - Timestamp) between (0min .. 5min)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

detection_queries.title: PsExec/smbexec-style Remote Service Execution (Cortex XDR)
detection_queries.description: Cortex XDR equivalent flagging PsExec/smbexec process signatures alongside admin-share file activity.
detection_queries.query:
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and event_sub_type = ENUM.PROCESS_START
| filter action_process_image_name ~= "psexec.*\.exe" or action_process_image_command_line contains "smbexec"
| fields agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, action_process_image_command_line, event_timestamp

false_positives: Legitimate software deployment and patch management tooling (SCCM, remote admin scripts) that uses admin shares as their normal mechanism
IT staff running approved remote maintenance via PsExec-style tools under a documented change ticket
response_steps: Identify the file transferred to the admin share and the execution mechanism (service/task/WMI) that followed
Trace the source host and account used for the SMB connection
Check every other host the same account or tool touched via the same pattern
Remove the malicious service/task and any dropped binaries; verify no additional persistence was staged in the same session

mitigations.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigations.detail: Restrict SMB communications using host firewall rules.

mitigations.name: Limit Access to Resource Over Network
mitigations.detail: Disable Windows administrative shares where not operationally required.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.detail: Enforce non-reusable, complex local admin passwords (LAPS).

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Deny remote use of local admin credentials; restrict local admin group membership.

related.name: Local Accounts
related.relation: Reused local admin passwords are a common credential source for admin-share access across many hosts.

related.name: Security Account Manager
related.relation: Where the local admin hash enabling this access is usually obtained.

hypothesis.statement: An executable is written to ADMIN$ or C$ over SMB, and a new service or scheduled task referencing that same file is created on the target within five minutes.
hypothesis.rationale: Hunt for the pairing, not the SMB write alone -- file copies to admin shares are routine in any environment running centralized software deployment, and the execution trigger that follows is what actually separates malicious use from routine patching.

subtechniques.name: Distributed Component Object Model
subtechniques.overview: DCOM extends Windows' Component Object Model over RPC, letting a client invoke methods on objects hosted on a remote machine. By default only administrators can remotely activate and launch COM objects, but a privileged user can leverage insecure methods on remotely-instantiated Office application objects to run macros, invoke Dynamic Data Exchange, or drive WMI — achieving code execution on a remote host without ever dropping a file to disk.

concepts.term: What DCOM actually lets a remote client do
concepts.explanation: COM lets one piece of software call methods on another running on the same machine; DCOM removes the same-machine requirement using RPC as the transport. Access is governed by registry-based ACLs, not a separate authentication step — if your account is permitted to launch and access a given COM object per those ACLs, the object runs with your privileges, remotely, with no separate exploit needed. Office application objects are a favorite target specifically because instantiating one remotely and driving it via COM can execute a macro or invoke DDE without a document ever being visibly opened.

DCOM activation always negotiates over RPC endpoint mapper traffic on TCP 135 before the actual object method call happens on a dynamically assigned port. That means a remote DCOM launch produces a consistent, protocol-level signature — inbound 135 traffic followed by activity on a high ephemeral port — regardless of which specific COM object or method is being abused, which is why network segmentation and Windows Firewall (which blocks DCOM by default) are effective mitigations independent of what the attacker is actually trying to do with it.

procedure_examples.activity: Delivers Beacon payloads for lateral movement by leveraging remote COM execution.
Utilizes Invoke-DCOM to leverage remote COM execution for lateral movement.
Uses System namespace methods to execute lateral movement via DCOM.

data_sources.detail: Inbound TCP 135 (RPC endpoint mapper) followed by activity on a dynamically assigned high port, the DCOM activation signature.
Office application processes (excel.exe, winword.exe) or mmc.exe/wmiprvse.exe spawning unexpectedly, with a remote-originated parent chain.
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Classes\AppID and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Ole permission changes, which govern who can remotely launch/access COM objects.

detection_queries.title: Suspicious Office Process Spawned via Remote DCOM Activation

mitigations.name: Application Isolation and Sandboxing

hypothesis.statement: Inbound RPC traffic to TCP 135 precedes an Office application process spawning without explorer.exe anywhere in its parent chain.
hypothesis.rationale: Neither signal alone is reliable -- RPC to 135 is common on any domain-joined network, and Office processes launch through many legitimate mechanisms -- but the combination, in that order, is specific enough to investigate directly.

subtechniques.name: SSH
subtechniques.overview: SSH ships on nearly every Linux and macOS system and can be enabled on ESXi hosts directly or via vCenter, giving an authenticated user a command-line session on the remote host with whatever privileges that account holds. Because SSH is the standard, expected admin tool on these platforms — unlike RDP on Windows, which ordinary users rarely touch — an SSH-based lateral movement session carries very little inherent suspicion on its own.

concepts.term: Why SSH abuse blends in more than RDP abuse does
concepts.explanation: On Windows, RDP usage by anyone other than IT is already somewhat unusual, which gives defenders a useful baseline. SSH is the opposite: it's the routine way legitimate administrators, deployment pipelines, and monitoring agents interact with Linux/macOS/ESXi hosts constantly. That means detection here can't lean on "SSH connection happened" at all — it has to focus entirely on who's connecting, from where, and what they do once inside, since the protocol itself is used identically by attackers and admins alike.

concepts.term: Salt Typhoon's loopback trick as a case study in ACL bypass
concepts.explanation: Salt Typhoon modified a compromised switch's loopback interface address specifically so their SSH connections would appear to originate from a trusted internal address rather than their real source — defeating access control lists scoped to "only accept SSH from these expected internal ranges." It's a concrete illustration of a broader point: source-IP-based SSH restrictions are only as strong as the assumption that the visible source IP reflects where a connection actually originated, and on network infrastructure the attacker already controls, that assumption can be deliberately broken.

concepts.term: Agent forwarding turns one compromised jump host into every host that trusts its users
concepts.explanation: When a user connects with SSH agent forwarding enabled, their local ssh-agent's private key never actually leaves their machine — but the agent creates a Unix socket on the intermediate host and exports its path via SSH_AUTH_SOCK, so anything with sufficient permission on that intermediate host to read the socket can relay signing requests through it and authenticate onward as that user, to every host that trusts their key, without the private key material itself ever being extracted or exposed. A root-level attacker on a jump host doesn't need to steal a key file at all; they just need to find and reuse someone else's forwarded agent socket while that person's session happens to be active, which is exactly why disabling agent forwarding (or using ProxyJump instead) closes this path entirely rather than just making key theft harder.

data_sources.detail: SSH logon events, especially for accounts or from sources inconsistent with that account's normal pattern; password-based auth where key-based is expected.

subtechniques.name: VNC
subtechniques.overview: VNC (Virtual Network Computing, using the RFB protocol) is screen-sharing rather than a full remote session negotiation — it mirrors an existing display rather than creating a new one the way RDP does. Since it isn't installed by default on Windows, VNC-based lateral movement often starts with the attacker dropping their own VNC server (TightVNC, UltraVNC) onto the target, which shifts the detection question toward "why does unexpected VNC server software exist here" rather than "is a built-in feature being abused."

concepts.explanation: RDP negotiates a session — it can create a brand-new desktop session independent of whoever's physically logged in. VNC's original design is to mirror the display that's already there, which in some configurations means the legitimate user's actual screen is literally what the attacker sees in real time, potentially without the user immediately noticing anything different is happening at all. That distinction is why VNC is sometimes preferred for reconnaissance-style lateral movement — watching what a user does — rather than pure command execution.

concepts.term: Why 'unexpected VNC server' is often the whole signal
concepts.explanation: Because Windows carries no built-in VNC server, its presence on a host at all is frequently the tell — legitimate remote-support VNC deployments are usually a known, inventoried, deliberate choice, not something that shows up unannounced. That's why the primary mitigations here are audit (find unauthorized installs) and limiting software installation rather than protocol-level restrictions the way RDP/SSH get: the fix is mostly about not letting the software exist in the first place.

subtechniques.name: Windows Remote Management
subtechniques.overview: WinRM is the Windows service and protocol that underlies PowerShell Remoting — Invoke-Command and Enter-PSSession use it by default — letting an authenticated user execute programs, modify the registry, manage services, and drive WMI on a remote host. Because it's PowerShell's own remoting mechanism, "PowerShell Remoting abuse" and "WinRM abuse" describe the exact same activity from two different angles.

concepts.explanation: Every remote PowerShell session — whether started via Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command, or a tool like Evil-WinRM — spawns commands under wsmprovhost.exe (the WinRM provider host process) on the target. The typical process chain is svchost.exe → wsmprovhost.exe → whatever the attacker actually ran. That makes wsmprovhost.exe as a parent process one of the most reliable single-process fingerprints in this entire pack, functionally playing the same role for WinRM that a specific LSASS GrantedAccess mask plays for T1003.001.

concepts.term: Why mitigating this means touching WinRM config, not PowerShell itself
concepts.explanation: Because PowerShell Remoting is WinRM under the hood, restricting it isn't a PowerShell-specific setting — it means disabling the WinRM service, tightening its TrustedHosts configuration, or firewalling ports 5985/5986 (HTTP/HTTPS). Someone trying to 'disable PowerShell Remoting' by touching PowerShell execution policy alone will find WinRM itself, and every other tool that rides on it, completely untouched.

procedure_examples.activity: Executed commands and payloads using PowerShell over WinRM.
Deployed the Evil-WinRM tool for PowerShell-based remote code execution.
Conducted lateral movement via Windows Remote Management.

detection_queries.title: Suspicious Child Process Under wsmprovhost.exe

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)

subtechniques.name: Cloud Services
subtechniques.overview: A synced or federated identity works against cloud consoles and CLIs (Azure PowerShell's Connect-AzAccount, Microsoft Graph's Connect-MgGraph, gcloud auth login) exactly the way it works on-premises, which means an attacker with valid cloud credentials can move from one cloud service to another — or from an on-prem foothold straight into cloud infrastructure — without needing any network adjacency to the target at all.

concepts.term: Federated identity dissolves the network-adjacency requirement
concepts.explanation: Every other sub-technique in this pack requires the attacker to actually reach the target over a network — the same segment, a routable path, something. Cloud console/CLI access requires none of that: a valid Azure AD, AWS IAM, or Google Workspace credential authenticates from anywhere on the internet directly to the cloud provider's own API. "Lateral movement" here means moving between services and privilege levels within the cloud tenant, not moving across physical or virtual network boundaries at all.

concepts.term: CLI-based access changes what telemetry actually exists
concepts.explanation: A lot of this activity is CLI-driven (Connect-AzAccount, gcloud auth login, aws configure) rather than an interactive console session with a browser fingerprint. That pushes almost all the relevant detection surface into cloud audit logs — sign-in events correlated with the API calls that follow — since there's no traditional network packet capture or endpoint process tree spanning the actual lateral hop the way there would be for RDP or SSH.

procedure_examples.activity: Leveraged compromised high-privileged on-premises accounts synced to Office 365 for lateral cloud movement via Azure AD PowerShell.
Used Azure credentials for lateral movement and exploited pre-existing AWS EC2 instances.
Utilized a compromised Entra Connect Sync Server for environment-wide lateral movement.
Accessed and propagated to AWS EC2 instances via SSM Send-Command.

data_sources.detail: Atypical geolocation or user-agent cloud logins followed immediately by resource or directory enumeration.

data_sources.source: Cloud audit logs (CloudTrail / Azure Activity / GCP Audit)
data_sources.detail: CLI-based authentication (Connect-AzAccount, gcloud auth login) from an unexpected source, correlated with the API calls that follow.
Mailbox or document access via CLI/API from a source inconsistent with that user's normal client application pattern.

detection_queries.title: CLI-Based Cloud Authentication from Unexpected Source
detection_queries.description: Flags Azure AD sign-ins using CLI/PowerShell client applications from a source IP or location outside the account's established pattern.
detection_queries.query:
SigninLogs
| where AppDisplayName in ("Azure PowerShell", "Azure CLI", "Microsoft Graph PowerShell")
| where ResultType == 0
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location=tostring(LocationDetails.city)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

false_positives: Legitimate DevOps/automation pipelines authenticating via CLI as part of normal infrastructure-as-code workflows
IT administrators using Azure/AWS/GCP CLI tools for approved remote administration from a home or travel location
response_steps: Identify the identity used and whether it's a synced/federated account bridging on-prem and cloud
Review the full sequence of API calls made after authentication, not just the sign-in event itself
Check for privilege escalation via role/policy changes made during the session
If Entra Connect or an equivalent sync service was involved, treat both cloud and on-premises environments as potentially affected

mitigations.name: Multi-factor Authentication
mitigations.detail: Apply MFA across all cloud services, including CLI-based authentication paths.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.detail: Prevent on-premises accounts from holding cloud permissions directly; use isolated cloud-only administrative accounts.

related.name: Cloud Accounts
related.relation: The credential compromise that makes this lateral movement path possible.

related.name: Cloud API
related.relation: The same CLI/API surface, viewed from the execution angle rather than the movement angle.

hypothesis.statement: A federated or synced identity authenticates to a cloud console or CLI (Connect-AzAccount, gcloud auth login) from a client or location it has never used in its prior sign-in history.
hypothesis.rationale: There is no network-layer corroboration available for this hypothesis the way there is for on-prem lateral movement -- cloud identity and sign-in logs are the entire evidentiary basis, so confirm they're actually being retained and queryable before committing to this hunt.

subtechniques.name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
subtechniques.overview: Cloud providers offer native, out-of-band ways to reach a VM's console directly — Azure Serial Console, AWS EC2 Instance Connect, AWS Systems Manager — that bypass the VM's actual network interface entirely, connecting through the cloud provider's own management plane instead. Several of these mechanisms are built for break-glass recovery scenarios and grant SYSTEM or root access by default, which means compromising the cloud identity that can invoke them is equivalent to already having full administrative access to the VM.

concepts.term: Why this bypasses network and host-based defenses entirely
concepts.explanation: Azure Serial Console, EC2 Instance Connect, and Systems Manager don't connect to the VM over its normal network interface at all — they connect through the cloud provider's control plane, out-of-band from anything the VM's own firewall, network security group, or NACLs could ever see or block. A host that's completely locked down at the network level is still fully reachable this way, because the connection was never subject to that network's rules in the first place.

concepts.term: Why default SYSTEM/root access is the real danger, not just the access itself
concepts.explanation: Unlike RDP or SSH, which authenticate as whatever account was used and grant that account's actual privileges, several of these features are specifically designed as an emergency recovery path and hand over SYSTEM or root by default regardless of the connecting identity's normal permissions. That means an attacker doesn't need a separate privilege escalation step once they can invoke the feature at all — the cloud IAM permission to use Serial Console or Instance Connect is itself equivalent to full administrative compromise of the target VM.

procedure_examples.activity: Leveraged SaaS and cloud environment access as part of broader cloud-native intrusion operations, consistent with abuse of native cloud VM connection methods.

data_sources.detail: Invocation of EC2 Instance Connect, Systems Manager Send-Command/Session, or Azure Serial Console access, correlated with the IAM identity that triggered it.
Permissions changes granting an identity access to these direct-connect features, which is itself worth monitoring as a precursor.

detection_queries.title: AWS Systems Manager Session Started on Production Instance
detection_queries.description: Flags SSM Start-Session/Send-Command invocations, a native direct-VM-access mechanism worth scoping to expected automation identities only.
detection_queries.query:
title: AWS SSM Session Started
id: 3d8b6a4c-9f2e-4c7a-8d1b-6f3a9c8e2d50
status: experimental
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: cloud
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    eventName:
      - 'StartSession'
      - 'SendCommand'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate automation/DevOps pipelines using SSM as their standard remote management mechanism
level: medium
tags:
  - attack.lateral_movement
  - attack.t1021.008

false_positives: Legitimate DevOps/automation pipelines that use Systems Manager or Instance Connect as their standard, approved VM access mechanism
Break-glass recovery use by cloud infrastructure administrators during a genuine outage
response_steps: Identify the IAM identity that invoked the direct-connect feature and how it obtained that permission
Treat this as equivalent to full administrative compromise of the target VM given the default SYSTEM/root access these features grant
Review IAM policy for how broadly this permission is granted and scope it down to only the automation identities that genuinely need it
Check CloudTrail/Activity logs for what commands were run during the session

mitigations.name: Disable or Remove Feature or Program
mitigations.detail: Deactivate direct VM connection features when not administratively necessary.

mitigations.name: User Account Management
mitigations.detail: Restrict IAM permissions for these native access methods to the minimum set of identities that require them.

related.name: Cloud Accounts
related.relation: The IAM identity compromise that grants the permission to invoke these direct connection features in the first place.

hypothesis.statement: EC2 Instance Connect, Systems Manager Send-Command/StartSession, or Azure Serial Console is invoked by an identity outside the organization's documented break-glass or automation allowlist.
hypothesis.rationale: Because several of these features grant SYSTEM or root by default regardless of the connecting identity's normal permissions, treat any unauthorized invocation as equivalent to full VM compromise rather than a finding that needs corroboration before escalating.
